title: Inside Pakistan's Power Shift: How Asim Munir Became the Most Powerful Man in Islamabad
excerpt: As three insurgencies merge and the US leans on Rawalpindi for Iran diplomacy, Field Marshal Munir's grip on Pakistan tightens while civilian governance withers.
body:
• Field Marshal Asim Munir has become Pakistan's most powerful military leader since Pervez Musharraf, holding the newly created Chief of Defence Forces position with lifetime legal immunity under the 27th Constitutional Amendment.
  • US President Donald Trump has reportedly bypassed PM Shehbaz Sharif in favour of Munir for back-channel US-Iran mediation, with negotiations coordinated from Rawalpindi rather than Islamabad.
  • Pakistan's three concurrent insurgencies — in Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and PoK — have merged into a deadlier security crisis, with militant attacks rising sharply in 2026.
  • The power consolidation raises alarm bells for India's strategic establishment and diaspora investors tracking South Asian geopolitical risk.

Pakistan's military establishment is tightening its grip on power at a pace not seen in nearly two decades, with Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir emerging as the country's dominant political force — and the civilian government of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif increasingly looking like an afterthought.

The Architecture of Military Supremacy

The 27th Constitutional Amendment, passed in November 2025, cemented the military's institutional dominance. It created a Chief of Defence Forces position held by the Army Chief, granting command over the Navy and Air Force, and provided lifetime legal immunity to five-star officers. For Munir — elevated to Field Marshal in May 2025 despite setbacks during Operation Sindoor against India — the amendment effectively places him above civilian oversight.

"The foreign ministry is just a junior partner. Countries like Iran and the US have this confidence in Asim Munir. Our government ministers are really an adjunct."

— Maleeha Lodhi, Pakistan's former ambassador to the UN, US, and UK, speaking to The Guardian

Munir's June 2025 visit to the White House made history: he became the first serving Pakistani military leader to meet a sitting US president without holding political office. The meeting included a formal lunch with Trump and discussions with US Cabinet members.

The US-Iran Mediation and Sharif's Sidelining

Pakistan has positioned itself as an unlikely diplomatic broker between Washington and Tehran, but the mediation is being coordinated from Rawalpindi — the seat of the army — rather than Islamabad. According to The Guardian, Trump directly leaned on Munir to leverage his ties with Iranian leadership. When US and Iranian delegations met in Islamabad, Munir was the third party in the room.

PM Sharif has publicly credited Munir with playing a "crucial role" in relaying messages between Washington and Tehran — a statement that analysts view less as generosity than as an acknowledgment of reality. Subsequent diplomatic forays, including Munir's Tehran visit accompanied by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, have reinforced the military's monopoly on foreign policy.

Three Wars Converging Into One Crisis

Compounding the political turbulence is a deepening security crisis. Data compiled by India Today and Pakistan Today shows Pakistan's three long-running insurgencies — in Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir — have merged into what analysts describe as a deadlier, more coordinated threat. Militant groups from the TTP, Baloch separatists, and PoK-based outfits are increasingly sharing logistics and intelligence, stretching the military thin across multiple fronts.

First-quarter 2026 data shows terror-related fatalities rose sharply compared to the same period in 2025, even as military operations in Waziristan and Balochistan continue. The army's internal challenges have not slowed Munir's consolidation of political power — if anything, they have provided justification for it.

What This Means for India and the Diaspora

For India's strategic establishment, the concentration of power in one military figure introduces both predictability and risk. Munir's rapport with Trump could shape the trajectory of US-Pakistan relations in ways that affect India's interests, from the Kashmir question to counterterrorism cooperation.

Analysts warn that if the US-Iran mediation succeeds, Munir's stature will be further elevated, deepening civilian marginalisation. If it fails, it could trigger internal backlash against the Sharif coalition and introduce fresh volatility in a nuclear-armed neighbour. For NRI investors with exposure to South Asian markets, the political instability premium on Pakistan has rarely been higher.

The International Commission of Jurists has termed the 27th Amendment an "attack on judicial independence." Yet Pakistan's political class, chastened by the example of Imran Khan's ouster and imprisonment, appears unwilling to challenge the military's expanding footprint.
